newsitem.title: UK: Russian Urals said stronger, Nigeria eyes Asia dem.
newsitem.headline: Russian Urals said stronger, Nigeria eyes Asia dem.

text.p: Mediterranean crude oil traders said on Tuesday that Russian Urals firmed but conflicting reports over a major recent deal lead some players to dismiss the price the sour crude fetched as unreal.
A Russian major was heard to have sold a Urals cargo on Tuesday at Dated Brent -$0.99 cif but no further details were available on the reported deal.
Some traders said they suspected the sour crude could have fetched this price and said the deal took place late last week and involded a cargo of some 140,000 tonnes which fetched -$1.07.
"I was very surprised by that figure (Dated Brent -$0.99)," one trader said. "Can I hear the word 'manipulation' perhaps? I don't know."

However, a deal on Monday under which a trading house bought a May 25-27 Urals at Dated Brent -$1.07 seemed to indicate the sour has firmed since it traded on Friday at Dated Brent -$1.18, -$1.25 and -$.135 respectively.
One of those deals included a Russian major selling a prompt cargo headed to Israel, priced at a $1.25 discount to Dated Brent and loading at the Black Sea Odessa port.
Earlier on Tuesday, a trader said that in an "unclear" market, buyers and sellers were talking May barrels as far apart as Dated Brent -$1.20 and -$1.05.
"There is some buying interest but I guess potential buyers are waiting just to see where the market is going because it is not very clear," a trader said, adding margins have worsened.

One Italian trader said there may be some Urals congestion by the end of May due to a scheduled closer of the main oil berth at Russia's main Novorossiisk port for maintenance May 20-23, in addition to the closer of two smaller berths for most of this month for repair work.
Earlier closures of Novorossiisk due to bad weather would aggravate the situation, the trader said.
A leading shipping source in London, seemingly confirming the trader's repport, said Novorossiisk's main Berth One may close for May 20-24 for maintenance.
The smaller Berth Two and Three, closed since May 6 for maintenance, will open on May 25, the source said.

Asked to comment on a trader's remarks that Berth One will close May 20-23, the source said: "It's quite possible, there have been shuttings due to maintenance for the last five months towards the end of the month.
"I haven't got official confirmation of it but it would fit in the pattern we have been seeing for the past four or five months."
The closure of Berth One would probably cause a two day delay in oil loadings, "but if it is scheduled and it is in the programme, I think people would have planned around it," the source added.

Berth One can load ships over 90,000 tonne deadweight while Berth Two, the second largest, can take ships from 60,000 to 90,000 tonnes deadweight. Berth Three is a small oil products berth. In a quiet West African market, traders said the recent rise in the price of benchmark Brent blend was causing some anxiety that Asian demand for West African barrels may wane.
The traders said no deals were heard on Tuesday but a U.S. refiner said it had bought on Monday a May 20 Nemba/Cabinda at about Dated Brent -5 cents and Dated Brent -$1.15 cents, respectively.
This was unchanged to slightly weeker than a deal last week at Dated Brent evens and -$1.15 respectively.
A French refiner said it fetched Dated Brent +45 cents fob for an early June Bonny Light on Monday.

Traders said the Nigerians, most of whose sweet crudes trade at a premium to Dated Brent, were a little worried that a recent flurry of Asian demand for their barrels may dip with the recent rise in Brent's price.
"The price of the Atlantic basin barrel, as the base price, has gone up so much that you may have restricted the movement to the East," one refiner said.
"The Far East players are saying at this price, we are going to wait," the refiner said.

He said on BQ the asking price was still a premium of some 50 cents to Dated Brent, adding a mid May Escarvos was offered on Monday at a premium of 44-46 cents to Dated Brent "whereas a few days ago you would see it offered at a few cents higher".
But he said the West African sours are a little bit more aggressive than they have been last week when they were "very, very lacklustre and low-key".

A European trading house said the market was not very nervous over Shell Nigeria's shut down of five oil flow stations due to tribal feuds, but added that players were watching to see how the situation develops.
A Shell spokesman in Lagos said the production of the five stations in southeast Nigeria was 120,000 barrels per day but that no force majeure had been declared.

Later in the day, Shell Nigeria said communal unrest in the oil-rich Niger Delta could develop into a crisis similar to the 1993 uprising which forced the company to abandon production in Ogoniland in the southeast.
--Haitham Haddadin, London newsroom +44 171 542 8145
